{{Short description|Area of research in mathematics (graph theory)}}
In [[graph theory]], '''perfect matching in high-degree hypergraphs''' is a research avenue trying to find [[Sufficient Condition|sufficient conditions]] for existence of a [[Matching in hypergraphs|perfect matching in a hypergraph]], based only on the [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] of vertices or subsets of them.

== Introduction ==

=== Degrees and matchings in graphs ===
In a simple [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}}, the [[degree of a vertex]] {{mvar|v}}, often denoted by {{math|deg(''v'')}} or {{math|δ(''v'')}}, is the number of edges in {{mvar|E}} adjacent to {{mvar|v}}. The minimum degree of a graph, often denoted by {{math|deg(''G'')}} or {{math|δ(''v'')}}, is the minimum of {{math|deg(''v'')}} over all vertices {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}}.

A [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] in a graph is a set of edges such that each vertex is adjacent to at most one edge; a '''perfect matching''' is a matching in which each vertex is adjacent to exactly one edge. A perfect matching does not always exist, and thus it is interesting to find sufficient conditions that guarantee its existence.

One such condition follows from [[Dirac's theorem on Hamiltonian cycles]]. It says that, if {{math|deg(''G'') ≥ {{frac|''n''|2}}}}, then the graph admits a [[Hamiltonian cycle]]; this implies that it admits a perfect matching. The factor {{math|{{frac|''n''|2}}}} is tight, since the [[complete bipartite graph]] on {{math|({{frac|''n''|2}} – 1, {{frac|''n''|2}} + 1)}} vertices has degree {{math|{{frac|''n''|2}} – 1}} but does not admit a perfect matching.

The results described below aim to extend these results from graphs to [[hypergraph]]s.

=== Degrees in hypergraphs ===
In a hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E)''}}, each edge of {{mvar|E}} may contain more than two vertices of {{mvar|V}}. The degree of a vertex {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}} is, as before, the number of edges in {{mvar|E}} that contain {{mvar|v}}. But in a hypergraph we can also consider the degree of ''subsets'' of vertices: given a subset {{mvar|U}} of {{mvar|V}}, {{math|deg(''U'')}} is the number of edges in {{mvar|E}} that contain ''all'' vertices of {{mvar|U}}. Thus, the degree of a hypergraph can be defined in different ways depending on the size of subsets whose degree is considered.

Formally, for every integer {{math|''d'' ≥ 1}}, {{math|deg{{sub|''d''}}(''H'')}} is the minimum of {{math|deg(''U'')}} over all subsets {{mvar|U}} of {{mvar|V}} that contain exactly {{mvar|d}} vertices. Thus, {{math|deg{{sub|1}}(''H'')}} corresponds to the  definition of a degree of a simple graph, namely the smallest degree of a single vertex; {{math|deg{{sub|2}}(''H'')}} is the smallest degree of a pair of vertices; etc.

A hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} is called '''{{mvar|r}}-uniform''' if every hyperedge in {{mvar|E}} contains exactly {{mvar|r}} vertices of {{mvar|V}}. In {{mvar|r}}-uniform graphs, the relevant values of {{mvar|d}} are {{math|1, 2, … , ''r'' – 1}}. In a simple graph, {{math|1=''r'' = 2}}.

== Conditions on 1-vertex degree ==
Several authors proved sufficient conditions for the case {{math|1=''d'' = 1}}, i.e., conditions on the smallest degree of a single vertex. 

* If {{mvar|H}} is a 3-uniform hypergraph on {{mvar|n}} vertices, {{mvar|n}} is a multiple of 3, and <p><math>\deg_1(H)\geq\bigg(5/9+o(1)\bigg){n\choose 2},</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a perfect matching.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Hàn|first1=Hip|last2=Person|first2=Yury|last3=Schacht|first3=Mathias|date=2009-01-01|title=On Perfect Matchings in Uniform Hypergraphs with Large Minimum Vertex Degree|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|language=en-US|volume=23|issue=2|pages=732–748|doi=10.1137/080729657|issn=0895-4801}}</ref></p>
* If {{mvar|H}} is a 3-uniform hypergraph on {{mvar|n}} vertices, {{mvar|n}} is a multiple of 3, and <p><math>\deg_1(H)\geq {n-1\choose 2} - {2n/3\choose 2}+1,</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a perfect matching - a matching of size {{mvar|k}}. This result is the best possible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Khan|first=Imdadullah|date=2013-01-01|title=Perfect Matchings in 3-Uniform Hypergraphs with Large Vertex Degree|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=27|issue=2|pages=1021–1039|doi=10.1137/10080796X|s2cid=18434210|issn=0895-4801}}</ref></p>
* If {{mvar|H}} is a 4-uniform hypergraph with on {{mvar|n}} vertices, {{mvar|n}} is a multiple of 4, and <p><math>\deg_1(H)\geq {n-1\choose 3} - {3n/4\choose 3},</math></p><p> then {{mvar|H}} contains a perfect matching - a matching of size {{mvar|k}}. This result is the best possible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Khan|first=Imdadullah|date=2016-01-01|title=Perfect matchings in 4-uniform hypergraphs|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B|language=en|volume=116|pages=333–366|doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2015.09.005|issn=0095-8956|doi-access=free|arxiv=1101.5675}}</ref></p>
* If {{mvar|H}} is {{mvar|r}}-uniform, n is a multiple of {{mvar|r}}, and <p><math>\deg_1(H)> \frac{r-1}{r}\left({\binom{n-1}{r-1}-\binom{n-kr-1}{r-1}} \right),</math></p><p> then {{mvar|H}} contains a matching of size at least {{math|''k'' + 1}}. In particular, setting {{math|1=''k'' = {{frac|''n''|''r''}} – 1}} gives that, if </p><p><math>\deg_1(H)> \frac{r-1}{r}\left({\binom{n-1}{r-1}-1} \right),</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a perfect matching.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Daykin|first1=David E.|last2=Häggkvist|first2=Roland|date=1981-02-01|title=Degrees giving independent edges in a hypergraph|journal=Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=23|issue=1|pages=103–109|doi=10.1017/S0004972700006924|issn=1755-1633|doi-access=free}}</ref></p>
* If {{mvar|H}} is {{mvar|r}}-uniform and {{mvar|r}}-partite, each side contains exactly {{mvar|n}} vertices, and <p><math>\deg_1(H)> \frac{r-1}{r}\left({n^{r-1}-(n-k)^{r-1}} \right),</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a matching of size at least {{math|''k'' + 1}}. In particular, setting {{math|1=''k'' = n – 1}} gives that if </p><p><math>\deg_1(H)> \frac{r-1}{r}\left({n^{r-1}-1} \right),</math></p><p> then {{mvar|H}} contains a perfect matching.<ref name=":4" /></p>

For comparison, [[Dirac's theorem on Hamiltonian cycles]] says that, if {{mvar|H}} is 2-uniform (i.e., a simple graph) and  
:<math>\deg_1(H) \geq {n-1\choose 1} - {n/2\choose 1} + 1  = n/2,</math>
then {{mvar|H}} admits a perfect matching.

== Conditions on (r-1)-tuple degree ==
Several authors proved sufficient conditions for the case {{math|1=''d'' = ''r'' – 1}}, i.e., conditions on the smallest degree of sets of {{math|''r'' – 1}} vertices, in {{mvar|r}}-uniform hypergraphs with {{mvar|n}} vertices.

=== In ''r''-partite ''r''-uniform hypergraphs ===
The following results relate to {{mvar|r}}-partite hypergraphs that have exactly {{mvar|n}} vertices on each side ({{mvar|rn}} vertices overall):

* If <math>\deg_{r-1}(H)\geq n/2 + \sqrt{2 n\log_2 n}</math><p>and {{math|''n'' ≥ 1000}}, then {{mvar|H}} has a perfect matching. This expression is smallest possible up to the lower-order term; in particular, {{math|{{frac|''n''|2}}}} is not sufficient.<ref name=":0" /></p>
* If <math>\deg_{r-1}(H)\geq n/r</math><p> then {{mvar|H}} admits a matching that covers all but at most {{math|''r'' – 2}} vertices in each vertex class of {{mvar|H}}. The {{math|{{frac|''n''|''r''}}}} factor is essentially the best possible.<ref name=":0" /></p>
* Let {{math|''V''{{sub|1}}, … , ''V{{sub|r}}''}} be the {{mvar|r}} sides of {{mvar|H}}. If the degree of every {{math|(''r'' – 1)}}-tuple in {{math|{{frac|''V''|''V''{{sub|1}}}}}} is strictly larger than {{math|{{frac|''n''|2}}}}, and the degree of every {{math|(''r'' – 1)}}-tuple in {{math|{{frac|''V''|''V''{{sub|''r''}}}}}} is at least {{math|{{frac|''n''|2}}}}, then {{mvar|H}} admits a perfect matching. <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Aharoni|first1=Ron|last2=Georgakopoulos|first2=Agelos|last3=Sprüssel|first3=Philipp|date=2009-01-01|title=Perfect matchings in r-partite r-graphs|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195669808000644|journal=European Journal of Combinatorics|language=en|volume=30|issue=1|pages=39–42|doi=10.1016/j.ejc.2008.02.011|issn=0195-6698|arxiv=0911.4008|s2cid=1092170}}</ref>

=== In general ''r''-uniform hypergraphs ===
* For every {{math|''γ'' > 0}}, when {{mvar|n}} is large enough, if <p><math>\deg_{r-1}(H) \geq (1/2+\gamma)n</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} is Hamiltonian, and thus contains a perfect matching.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rödl|first1=Vojtěch|last2=Szemerédi|first2=Endre|last3=Ruciński|first3=Andrzej|date=2008-03-01|title=An approximate Dirac-type theorem for k-uniform hypergraphs|journal=Combinatorica|language=en|volume=28|issue=2|pages=229–260|doi=10.1007/s00493-008-2295-z|s2cid=5799411|issn=1439-6912}}</ref></p>
* If <math>\deg_{r-1}(H)\geq n/2 + 3 r^2 \sqrt{n\log_2 n}</math><p>and {{mvar|n}} is sufficiently large, then {{mvar|H}} admits a perfect matching.<ref name=":0" /></p>
* If <math>\deg_{r-1}(H)\geq n/r + 3 r^2 \sqrt{n\log_2 n},</math><p>then {{mvar|H}} admits a matching that covers all but at most {{math|2''r''<sup>2</sup>}} vertices. <ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Kühn|first1=Daniela|last2=Osthus|first2=Deryk|date=2006|title=Matchings in hypergraphs of large minimum degree|journal=Journal of Graph Theory|language=en|volume=51|issue=4|pages=269–280|doi=10.1002/jgt.20139|s2cid=6769560 |issn=1097-0118}}</ref></p>
* When {{mvar|n}} is divisible by {{mvar|r}} and sufficiently large, the threshold is <p><math>\deg_{r-1}(H)\geq n/2 - r + c_{k,n}</math></p><p>where {{math|''c''{{sub|''k'',''n''}}}} is a constant depending on the parity of {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|k}} (all expressions below are the best possible):<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Rödl|first1=Vojtech|last2=Ruciński|first2=Andrzej|last3=Szemerédi|first3=Endre|date=2009-04-01|title=Perfect matchings in large uniform hypergraphs with large minimum collective degree|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|language=en|volume=116|issue=3|pages=613–636|doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2008.10.002|issn=0097-3165|doi-access=free}}</ref></p>
** 3 when {{math|{{frac|''r''|2}}}} is even and {{math|{{frac|''n''|''r''}}}} is odd;
** {{frac|5|2}} when {{mvar|r}} is odd and {{math|{{frac|(''n''-1)|2}}}} is odd;
** {{frac|3|2}} when {{mvar|r}} is odd and {{math|{{frac|(''n''-1)|2}}}} is even;
** 2 otherwise.
* When {{mvar|n}} is not divisible by {{mvar|r}}, the sufficient degree is close to {{math|{{frac|''n''|''r''}}}}: if {{math|deg{{sub|''r''-1}}(''H'')  ≥  {{frac|''n''|''r''}} + ''O''(log(''n''))}}, then {{mvar|H}} admits a perfect matching. The expression is almost the smallest possible: the smallest possible is {{math|⌊{{frac|''n''|''r''}}⌋}}.<ref name=":1" />

== Other conditions ==
There are some sufficient conditions for other values of {{mvar|d}}:

* For all {{math|''d'' ≥ {{frac|''r''|2}}}}, the threshold for {{math|deg{{sub|''d''}}(''H'')}} is close to:<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Pikhurko|first=Oleg|date=2008-09-01|title=Perfect Matchings and K 4 3 -Tilings in Hypergraphs of Large Codegree|journal=Graphs and Combinatorics|volume=24|issue=4|pages=391–404|doi=10.1007/s00373-008-0787-7|s2cid=29248979|issn=0911-0119}}</ref><p><math>\left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{r-d}.</math></p>
* For all {{math|''d'' < {{frac|''r''|2}}}}, the threshold for {{math|deg{{sub|''d''}}(''H'')}} is at most:<ref name=":3" /><p><math>\left(\frac{r-d}{r}+o(1)\right)\binom{n-d}{r-d}</math></p>
* If {{mvar|H}} is {{mvar|r}}-partite and each side contains exactly {{mvar|n}} vertices, and <p><math>\deg_d(H) \geq \frac{r-d}{r}n^{r-d} + r n^{r-d-1},</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a matching covering all but {{math|(''d'' – 1)''r''}} vertices.<ref name=":3" /></p>
* If {{mvar|n}} is sufficiently large and divisible by {{mvar|r}}, and <p><math>\deg_d(H) \geq \frac{r-d}{r}\binom{n}{r-d} + r^{r+1}(\ln{n})^{1/2}n^{r-d-1/2},</math></p><p>then {{mvar|H}} contains a matching covering all but {{math|(''d'' – 1)''r''}} vertices.<ref name=":3" /></p>
